newsitem.title: USA: Clinton seeks change in tobacco pact with states.
newsitem.headline: Clinton seeks change in tobacco pact with states.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton Wednesday rejected as "unreasonable" part of the proposed tobacco deal that would restrict the government's hard-won powers to regulate nicotine and said it should be changed.

Speaking in Madrid after a NATO summit, Clinton said the proposed settlement between the tobacco industry and the 40 states suing it ought to be changed because it imposed an "unreasonable restriction" on regulation of tobacco by the federal Food and Drug Administration.
It was Clinton's first public repudiation of a part of the $368.5 billion deal with the tobacco industry. But he also said there were many good things in the landmark deal.
Clinton focused his comments on a narrow aspect of the FDA language when asked for his views in Madrid.

"I have reached only one conclusion about the settlement in terms of what has to be changed -- that portion that restricts the jurisdiction of the FDA in terms of limiting tobacco content in cigarettes or banning it outright ... because of some black market that might be created," he said.
"I do think that is a change that ought to be made and I cannot believe the tobacco companies would bring down the entire settlement over that," he said.
Reacting to the comments, five tobacco companies said they believed the proposed settlement reached with state attorneys general last month should be kept intact.
"We look forward to the opportunity to make the case for keeping intact the provisions of the proposed resolution as negotiated," the companies said in a statement.

Separately, former U.S. Surgeon General Everett Koop and former Food and Drug Administration Commissioner David Kessler presented the White House with an alternative approach charted by leading U.S. public health groups that would be tougher on the cigarette industry.

"There are now two documents on the table," Kessler told reporters outside the White House. "There is the (industry) settlement document, and today there is a document by the public health community."
The FDA's jurisdiction over nicotine was recently upheld by a federal court, and health advocates are adamant that any settlement not dilute it.

A White House task force is conducting a 30-day review of the proposed deal, which would require the companies to pay $368.5 billion over 25 years. Some of those funds would be earmarked for public health and anti-smoking programmes.

The accord requires the industry to recognise FDA authority but critics say the language creates loopholes and sets impossible standards for the FDA. For instance, the FDA could not phase out nicotine unless it could guarantee that no black market would emerge, the provision Clinton mentioned.

The Koop-Kessler panel stressed what it called severe shortcomings in the FDA part of the agreement. Its report may influence some members of Congress, which needs to pass legislation for the settlement to take effect.

"There should be no limitations on or special exception to FDA authority to regulate nicotine, other constituents and ingredients of tobacco products and such a no-limitations policy should be made completely explicit," the report said.

Koop and Kessler said their report was not a line-by-line critique of the proposed settlement but a blueprint for a good tobacco policy. The 70-page report also includes targets for cutting youth smoking that are more stringent than the settlement and tougher penalties if the goals are not met.
"It's not a criticism of any settlement that has been proposed by the industry," Koop said. "It is instead a template of what would be the best for a tobacco control policy for this country."
"If there is to be a settlement, the public health measures must be very strong. They must work in reducing the number of people, especially children, who smoke," Kessler said.

The two stressed they were more interested in the future of public health than in wringing money from the industry. "The only thing that should matter is the number of people who smoke in this country. It should not be about money," said Kessler, now dean of Yale's medical school.

Tobacco executives last week met with White House advisers and were not enthusiastic about reopening negotiations on the settlement but also did not rule out further concessions. More public health groups will be consulted this week.

The heads of Clinton's task force, Secretary of Health and Human Services Donna Shalala and White House domestic policy adviser Bruce Reed, said the Koop-Kessler committee made some "good recommendations" that would be taken into consideration.

Tobacco stocks fell, with Phillip Morris Cos. off $1 to $43.44, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco parent RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp. down 56 cents to $32.06, Loews Corp., which owns Lorillard Tobacco Co., down $1.06 to $102.125, and United States Tobacco Co. parent UST Inc. off 75 cents to $27.75, all on the New York Stock Exchange.
